title: Learn the halal and haram basics
whyMatters: Halal means permitted and haram means prohibited. The two ideas reach into a lot of areas, but food is the practical place to start. What you can and cannot eat comes up every single day, so getting comfortable with it early makes the rest easier. Most food, as it turns out, is halal. The rules are short, and Toronto has more halal options than you could work through in a year. It helps to treat the guidelines as a way of paying attention at every meal rather than a list of things taken away from you.

subSteps: Pork and pork products (bacon, ham, gelatin from pork) are haram.
Alcohol and other intoxicants are haram, and that covers drinks, cooking wine, and food made with alcohol.
Meat has to be halal-slaughtered (zabiha), which means the animal is killed humanely with Allah's name mentioned.
Seafood is generally halal, including fish and shrimp.
Fruits, vegetables, grains, dairy, and eggs are halal.
Most processed food is halal, though it is worth checking for gelatin, lard, or alcohol-based flavorings.
Look for halal certification symbols on the packaging. Common ones in Canada are IFANCC, ISNA, and HMA.
Scan the ingredients for gelatin (often from pork), lard, animal shortening, alcohol, and vanilla extract, which can contain alcohol.
When you are not sure, look the product up online or pick a certified halal alternative.
Plenty of mainstream brands are fine, and you will learn which ones fast.
Toronto has hundreds of halal restaurants and grocery stores.
Halal butchers sell properly slaughtered meat, so ask around your community for a recommendation.
Many of the big grocery chains carry a halal meat section.
Food delivery apps let you filter for halal restaurants.
International grocery stores, Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African, usually carry a wide range of halal products.

exactActions.text: See where else halal and haram apply
subSteps: The two categories cover behavior, business dealings, and relationships as well as food.
The principle is that everything is halal unless it has been specifically prohibited.
Something is haram because it causes harm, whether to your body, your soul, or the people around you.
Between the clearly halal and the clearly haram sit the doubtful matters (mashbooh). When you are unsure, the safer choice is to leave it.
These distinctions take time to learn. Hold on to the clear-cut rules first.
Your whole diet does not have to turn over in a week.
Start by cutting the clearest ones: pork and alcohol.
Then move across to halal meat.
Look for halal versions of your favorite foods, because most of them exist.
Be patient with yourself at social meals where your options are thin.

timeEstimate: Ongoing. The basic rules take a day, the full change takes weeks

obstacles.problem: It's hard to find halal food in my area
obstacles.solution: Toronto is one of the best cities in North America for halal food, though your immediate neighborhood may not show it. You can order halal meat online or buy in bulk from a butcher, and many converts stock up on one weekly trip. Vegetarian and seafood options are halal and available everywhere. When you eat out, a vegetarian dish at any restaurant is a safe bet.

This one is common and delicate. You can offer to cook your own meals or bring a halal dish to family dinners. Explain what you need gently, because most families come round given time. You can eat the vegetables and grains from a family meal and bring your own protein. Plenty of converts end up using cooking as the way they share this with their family.

obstacles.problem: I feel overwhelmed by all the rules
obstacles.solution: Start simple. No pork, no alcohol, halal meat. The rest you can pick up gradually. Do not try to become an expert on food additives this month. And if you eat something haram without knowing, there is no sin on you, because Allah judges your intention and your effort rather than your accidents.

obstacles.problem: I miss certain foods I used to eat
obstacles.solution: Missing familiar food is normal. Halal versions of almost everything exist: halal pepperoni, turkey bacon, non-alcoholic drinks, halal marshmallows. Toronto has specialty stores and online shops for exactly this. Your tastes will shift over time and you will end up with new favorites.

Eating with coworkers or friends who do not eat halal can feel uncomfortable at first. You do not have to make an announcement about it. Order what works for you off the menu. If someone asks, a short answer is usually met with respect. Most restaurants will accommodate a dietary need if you ask, and planning ahead for a social meal takes most of the stress out.

tinyVersion: Two rules to start with: no pork, no alcohol. The rest you can learn step by step. Most of what you already eat is probably halal anyway.
unlocksNext: With halal and haram in hand, you are ready to learn about fasting, which brings your body into the practice alongside your heart.
